policy.question: Hospital B (Dubai) and Hospitals A and C (Abu Dhabi) now see each other's medication data for the same patient under the patient's own grants. Which UAE federal, Dubai and Abu Dhabi rules govern this sharing, and do they treat patient consent the same way?

requirements.statement: Under UAE Federal Law Executive Regulations, disclosing a patient's health information to any party without the consent of the patient or their legal representative is legally prohibited, unless permitted by applicable legislation in force in the UAE.
Under Dubai Health Authority (DHA) Policy, sharing health information between non-affiliated entities in the UAE via Health Information Exchanges (NABIDH, Malaffi, Riayati) requires patient consent.
Under DHA Standards, patient consent for accessing health information systems remains valid for one year following the patient's last health encounter, unless explicitly revoked.

Under DHA Standards, patients must be informed of the potential consequences of not sharing health information and retain the right to withdraw consent and opt out, though withdrawal does not affect prior lawful access or incorporation of information into facility records.

Under Abu Dhabi Department of Health (DoH) Policy, healthcare facilities are mandated to share patient data with the Abu Dhabi Health Information Exchange (Malaffi) under universal participation goals and must seek patient consent by incorporating standard consent wording into healthcare facility consent forms.

policy.question: The patient has withdrawn consent for one hospital's records and opted out of the Dubai health information exchange. What do the rules say about the effect of withdrawal, including on information that was already shared?

requirements.statement: In Dubai, the withdrawal of consent does not affect any sharing of health information that was carried out under consent prior to the withdrawal.

Entities that have accessed or received health information via the Health Information System (HIS) prior to the revocation of consent and have incorporated such information into their own records may retain that information.
Patients have the right to withdraw consent and opt-out of the NABIDH exchange after being informed of the potential consequences of not sharing information.
Upon a patient's request, the DHA NABIDH team is responsible for opting the patient out of the NABIDH exchange.

policy.question: A clinician at an Abu Dhabi hospital requests emergency access to this patient's records held by a Dubai hospital. The patient has revoked the sharing grants and opted out of the Dubai exchange. What do the rules say about emergency access here, and are there conflicts or unclear points?

requirements.statement: In Dubai, 'Break The Glass' is defined as a mechanism allowing health professionals to gain access to protected health information (PHI) in the health information system (HIS) without the patient's consent.

In Abu Dhabi, authorized users may 'break the seal' if they determine in their reasonable judgment that the patient is in immediate need of medical attention and the information held by or accessible via the ADHIE platform may be material to emergency treatment.

gaps.title: Responsibility for cross-emirate medication safety coordination
gaps.description: There is no provision in the provided knowledge base that specifies which institution is responsible for coordinating follow-up on high-severity medication safety findings when the involved prescribers operate across different emirates (e.g., Abu Dhabi and Dubai).
gaps.recommendation: Consult the specific clinical governance frameworks or inter-emirate health data exchange agreements between the Department of Health (Abu Dhabi) and the Dubai Health Authority.
searched_queries: responsibility for coordinating follow-up medication safety across emirates
gaps.note: Not found in the ingested knowledge base; this is not proof that no rule exists.

comparisons.statement: The EU EHDS regulation (Article 20) provides a mechanism for designating a lead authority when multiple digital health authorities exist within a Member State, requiring one to be responsible for reporting and coordinating information from others.

caveats: The provided knowledge base contains general HIE policy for Abu Dhabi (DoH Policy 2020) emphasizing that patient safety is the responsibility of all stakeholders, but it does not address the specific jurisdictional coordination of cross-emirate clinical safety alerts.

The limitation regarding the patient's choice to withhold data from Hospital B (Dubai) further complicates the safety assessment, but no specific rule was found regarding the impact of such patient-initiated data restrictions on the duty to coordinate clinical follow-up.
